title: Why do some U.S. states change clocks while others don't?
sources: Department of Transportation Uniform Time Act
Congressional Research Service Daylight Saving Time

lines.text: Every March and November, Americans scramble to change their clocks, except in two entire states.
lines.caps: Why do some US states *never | change their *clocks?

lines.text: Hawaii and almost all of Arizona refuse to observe Daylight Saving Time.
The federal Uniform Time Act of nineteen sixty-six allows states to opt out of moving clocks forward.
lines.caps: Federal law allows states to *opt out | of springing *forward

lines.text: Hawaii sits close to the equator, where day length barely changes throughout the four seasons anyway.
lines.caps: Hawaii has identical day *length | all year *round

lines.text: In scorching Arizona, adding an extra hour of blistering sunlight in the hot evening is the last thing residents want.
lines.caps: Arizona doesn't want *extra | boiling sun in the *evening!

lines.text: Extra daylight in Phoenix means blasting expensive air conditioning an extra hour during summer heatwaves.
lines.caps: Extra sun means *more expensive | electricity and air *conditioning

lines.text: Would you prefer year-round permanent daylight time, or should we keep changing the clocks?
lines.caps: Should we end *clock changes | forever? Let us *know!
